# Getting Your Competition Data Out of MongoDB Atlas and Into R {#sec-mongodb-connect}

::: {.callout-note title="Why this matters"}
You can't analyse the dataset until you can pull it out of Atlas and into a tidy
data frame. Working through this before the event means the connection and
package setup aren't things you're debugging on the day.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
The starter template's `src/main.R` (@sec-starter-template) has an empty
`connect_to_db()` function waiting for you --- that's where the connection code
below goes.
:::

This sheet walks you through connecting to the competition's MongoDB Atlas
cluster from R, pulling the data down into a tidy data frame, and doing text
analysis on it with the tidyverse / tidytext ecosystem. It's written against the
actual schema you've been given (this is the AI Incident Database schema), so
the field names below match what you'll actually see. Work through it top to
bottom before the competition starts so the connection and package setup is one
less thing to debug on the day.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 1. What you'll need

- R (4.x) and RStudio (or Positron / VS Code with the R extension)
- The connection string for your Atlas cluster (competition organisers will give
  you this , it looks like
  `mongodb+srv://<username>:<password>@ai-incident-database.ugkyb5n.mongodb.net/`)
- The database name is 'aiidprod'

Install the packages you'll need once, up front:

```r
install.packages(c(
  "mongolite",   # connect to MongoDB and pull data into R
  "tidyverse",   # dplyr, purrr, ggplot2, tidyr, etc.
  "tidytext",    # tokenisation, sentiment lexicons, tf-idf
  "jsonlite",    # handling nested JSON/BSON fields
  "textclean",   # cleaning up messy text (contractions, HTML, etc.)
  "wordcloud2",  # optional, for word cloud visuals
  "widyr"        # optional, for word-pair / correlation analysis
))
```

`mongolite` is the key package here, it's the simplest way to talk to MongoDB
from R and it hands data back as a data frame, which is exactly the shape
tidyverse tools expect.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 2. Know your collections before you connect

The schema you were given defines several collections. The two you'll care about
for text analysis are:

- **`reports`** --- the actual documents/articles. This is where the free text
  lives. Key fields:
  - `_id` (objectId), `report_number` (number) --- `report_number` is the
    human-friendly key used to link a report to the incident(s) it belongs to
  - `title`, `text`, `plain_text` --- `text` may retain markdown/HTML formatting
    from the original source; `plain_text` is the cleaned version and is almost
    always what you want for tokenising/sentiment work
  - `description` --- a short editor-written summary, separate from the report
    body
  - `authors`, `submitters` --- arrays of strings
  - `tags` --- array of free-text tags
  - `language`, `source_domain`, `url`
  - `date_published`, `date_submitted`, `date_downloaded`, `date_modified`
  - `embedding` --- a precomputed vector embedding of the text (nested object
    with a `vector` field); you generally won't need to touch this unless you're
    doing similarity/clustering work directly on the provided vectors
  - `is_incident_report` (boolean)

- **`incidents`** --- the higher-level "event" that one or more reports are
  describing. Key fields:
  - `_id` (objectId), `incident_id` (number)
  - `title`, `description`, `date`
  - `reports` --- an **array of `report_number` values** (not full documents)
    pointing back into the `reports` collection --- this is how you join the two
    collections
  - `Alleged deployer of AI system`, `Alleged developer of AI system`,
    `Alleged harmed or nearly harmed parties` --- arrays of entity-name strings
  - `implicated_systems` --- array of strings
  - `editors`, `editor_notes`

- **`classifications`** --- tagging/label data (an `attributes` field) that
  links back to `incidents`/`reports` by their IDs --- useful if you want to
  bring in categorical labels alongside the report text.

- **`entities`** --- a lookup table of named entities (`entity_id`, `name`)
  referenced by the "alleged deployer/developer/harmed parties" fields above.

For most text-analysis tasks, you'll mainly work with `reports.plain_text`,
optionally joined to `incidents` for grouping/labels.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 3. Connect to the cluster

Never hard-code your username and password directly into a script you might
commit to GitHub or share with teammates. Use an `.Renviron` file instead.

**Create/edit your `.Renviron` file** (run this once):

```r
usethis::edit_r_environ()
```

Add a line like this, save, and restart R:

```
MONGO_URI="mongodb+srv://myusername:mypassword@ai-incident-database.ugkyb5n.mongodb.net/"
```

**Now connect from your script** --- one connection object per collection:

```r
library(mongolite)

db_name <- "aiidprod"  

reports_conn <- mongo(collection = "reports", db = db_name,
                       url = Sys.getenv("MONGO_URI"))

incidents_conn <- mongo(collection = "incidents", db = db_name,
                         url = Sys.getenv("MONGO_URI"))

# quick sanity check
reports_conn$count()
incidents_conn$count()
```

If `$count()` returns a number rather than an error, you're connected.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 4. Pulling data out

### 4.1 Grab the fields you actually need

Don't pull every field (especially not `embedding`, which is a large numeric
vector per document) if you don't need it. Use the `fields` argument to project
server-side:

```r
library(tidyverse)

report_cols <- '{
    "_id": 1, "report_number": 1, "title": 1, "plain_text": 1,
    "description": 1, "tags": 1, "authors": 1, "language": 1,
    "source_domain": 1, "date_published": 1
  }'


reports <- reports_conn$find(
  fields = report_cols) |> as_tibble()

glimpse(reports)
```

### 4.2 Filter server-side

`mongolite` accepts standard MongoDB query syntax as a JSON string, e.g. to grab
only English-language reports:

```r
reports_en <- reports_conn$find(
  query  = '{"language": "en"}',
  fields = '{"_id": 1, "report_number": 1, "title": 1, "plain_text": 1}'
) |> as_tibble()
```

For more information on the query syntax visit,
<https://jeroen.github.io/mongolite/query-data.html#query-syntax>

### 4.3 Pull the incidents and join on `report_number`

`incidents$reports` is an array of `report_number`s, not embedded report
documents, so joining means unnesting that array and matching it up:

```r
incidents <- incidents_conn$find(
  fields = '{
    "_id": 1, "incident_id": 1, "title": 1, "description": 1, "date": 1,
    "reports": 1, "Alleged deployer of AI system": 1,
    "Alleged developer of AI system": 1,
    "Alleged harmed or nearly harmed parties": 1
  }'
) |> as_tibble()

# one row per (incident_id, report_number) pair
incident_report_map <- incidents |>
  select(incident_id, reports) |>
  unnest_longer(reports) |>
  rename(report_number = reports)

# now every report row can carry its incident's metadata
reports_with_incident <- reports |>
  left_join(incident_report_map, by = "report_number") |>
  left_join(
    incidents |> select(incident_id, incident_title = title, date),
    by = "incident_id"
  )
```

### 4.4 Aggregation pipelines (optional, for heavier lifting)

For grouping/counting server-side before pulling data down:

```r
reports_per_year <- reports_conn$aggregate('[
  { "$group": {
      "_id": { "$substr": ["$date_published", 0, 4] },
      "n": { "$sum": 1 }
  }},
  { "$sort": { "_id": 1 } }
]') |> as_tibble()
```

### 4.5 Other nested/array fields

Several fields come back from `mongolite` as **list-columns**: `authors`,
`submitters`, `tags` (on `reports`); the "alleged deployer/developer/harmed
parties" fields (on `incidents`). Each of these is a simple *array of strings
per document*, so `unnest_longer()` is usually what you want (not
`unnest_wider()`, which is for nested *objects*):

```r
reports_authors <- reports |>
  select(report_number, authors) |>
  unnest_longer(authors)   # one row per (report_number, author)

incidents_parties <- incidents |>
  select(incident_id, `Alleged harmed or nearly harmed parties`) |>
  unnest_longer(`Alleged harmed or nearly harmed parties`) |>
  rename(harmed_party = `Alleged harmed or nearly harmed parties`)
```

Guard against missing/empty text before tokenising:

```r
reports <- reports |>
  mutate(plain_text = replace_na(plain_text, ""))
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 5. Cleaning the text

`plain_text` is already stripped of most markup, but scraped news text still
tends to carry boilerplate (bylines, "read more" links, share-button text). Do a
light cleaning pass and keep the original column in case later analysis needs
it:

::: {.callout-warning}
The following is only a suggestion and is not guaranteed to produce fully
cleaned text ready for analysis.
:::

```r
library(textclean)

reports <- reports |>
  mutate(
    text_clean = plain_text |>
      replace_contraction() |>          # "don't" -> "do not"
      replace_url() |>
      replace_html() |>
      str_squish()                       # trim/collapse whitespace
  )
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 6. Tokenising with tidytext

`tidytext` works on the "one-token-per-row" principle, which plugs directly into
`dplyr`/`ggplot2`.

```r
library(tidytext)

tokens <- reports |>
  select(report_number, text_clean) |>
  unnest_tokens(word, text_clean)

# remove stop words
tokens_clean <- tokens |>
  anti_join(stop_words, by = "word")
```

### 6.1 Word frequencies

```r
top_words <- tokens_clean |>
  count(word, sort = TRUE)

top_words |>
  slice_max(n, n = 20) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(word, n), y = n)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "count", title = "Most frequent words across reports")
```

### 6.2 TF-IDF (which words distinguish one incident/domain from another)

This is a natural fit here: use `incident_id` or `source_domain` as the grouping
variable to see what language is distinctive to a given incident or outlet.

```r
tfidf <- reports_with_incident |>
  select(report_number, incident_id, text_clean) |>
  unnest_tokens(word, text_clean) |>
  anti_join(stop_words, by = "word") |>
  count(incident_id, word, sort = TRUE) |>
  bind_tf_idf(word, incident_id, n)

tfidf |>
  group_by(incident_id) |>
  slice_max(tf_idf, n = 10) |>
  ungroup()
```

### 6.3 N-grams

For phrase-level patterns rather than single words:

```r
bigrams <- reports |>
  unnest_tokens(bigram, text_clean, token = "ngrams", n = 2) |>
  separate(bigram, into = c("word1", "word2"), sep = " ") |>
  filter(!word1 %in% stop_words$word, !word2 %in% stop_words$word) |>
  count(word1, word2, sort = TRUE)
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 7. Sentiment analysis

`tidytext` bundles several sentiment lexicons (`bing`, `afinn`, `nrc`,
`loughran`). Join tokens to a lexicon the same way you joined stop words.
`loughran` is worth knowing about here specifically --- it was built for
financial/news text and includes categories like "uncertainty" and "litigious",
which can be more informative than generic positive/negative for news-style
incident reports.

```r
sentiment_scores <- tokens_clean |>
  inner_join(get_sentiments("bing"), by = "word") |>
  count(report_number, sentiment) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = sentiment, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) |>
  mutate(net_sentiment = positive - negative)
```

For a numeric score per word (rather than positive/negative labels), use
`afinn`:

```r
afinn_scores <- tokens_clean |>
  inner_join(get_sentiments("afinn"), by = "word") |>
  group_by(report_number) |>
  summarise(sentiment_score = sum(value), .groups = "drop")
```

`get_sentiments()` will prompt a one-time download/license confirmation the
first time you use a given lexicon --- do this well before the competition
starts, not on the day, in case you don't have internet access at the venue.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 8. Word co-occurrence / correlation (optional, `widyr`)

Useful for exploring which words tend to appear together within the same report:

```r
library(widyr)

word_pairs <- tokens_clean |>
  pairwise_count(word, report_number, sort = TRUE)

word_cors <- tokens_clean |>
  group_by(word) |>
  filter(n() >= 20) |>          # drop very rare words first
  pairwise_cor(word, report_number, sort = TRUE)
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 9. Putting it together: a minimal end-to-end script

```r
library(mongolite)
library(tidyverse)
library(tidytext)
library(textclean)

db_name <- "your_database_name"
reports_conn <- mongo(collection = "reports", db = db_name,
                       url = Sys.getenv("MONGO_URI"))

reports <- reports_conn$find(
  fields = '{"_id": 1, "report_number": 1, "title": 1, "plain_text": 1, "tags": 1}'
) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(
    plain_text = replace_na(plain_text, ""),
    text_clean = str_squish(replace_contraction(replace_url(plain_text, "")))
  )

word_counts <- reports |>
  unnest_tokens(word, text_clean) |>
  anti_join(stop_words, by = "word") |>
  count(word, sort = TRUE)

word_counts |> slice_max(n, n = 15)
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 10. Common pitfalls

- **Connection refused / timeout** --- your IP isn't allow-listed in Atlas
  Network Access, or you're on a network (uni wifi, VPN) that blocks the MongoDB
  port. Test the connection *before* the competition.
- **Pulling `embedding` by accident** --- it's a full numeric vector per
  document; leave it out of your `fields` projection unless you specifically
  need it, or your `find()` calls will be slow and memory-heavy.
- **Using `text` instead of `plain_text`** --- `text` can retain markdown/HTML
  from the original source, which will pollute your tokens (`<`, `##`, `href=`,
  etc.). Prefer `plain_text` for tokenising.
- **`unnest_wider()` on the wrong field** --- `authors`, `tags`, and the
  "alleged parties" fields are arrays of *strings*, so they need
  `unnest_longer()`. `unnest_wider()` is for fields that are nested *objects*
  (there aren't many of those in `reports`/`incidents`).
- **Joining `incidents` to `reports` on the wrong key** --- `incidents.reports`
  holds `report_number` values, not `_id` (objectId) values. Join on
  `report_number`, not `_id`.
- **Encoding issues (garbled characters)** --- check `Encoding()` on your text
  column and re-encode with `iconv()` if you see mojibake.
- **Credentials in scripts** --- always use `Sys.getenv()` against an
  `.Renviron` file, never paste the connection string directly into a script
  you'll share or commit.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 11. Quick reference: package cheat sheet

  | Task                   | Package       | Key function(s)                                            |
  | ---------------------- | ------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
  | Connect to MongoDB     | mongolite     | `mongo()`, `$find()`, `$aggregate()`, `$count()`           |
  | Wrangle data           | dplyr / tidyr | `mutate()`, `filter()`, `unnest_longer()`, `left_join()`   |
  | Clean text             | textclean     | `replace_contraction()`, `replace_url()`, `replace_html()` |
  | Tokenise               | tidytext      | `unnest_tokens()`                                          |
  | Frequency / TF-IDF     | tidytext      | `count()`, `bind_tf_idf()`                                 |
  | Sentiment              | tidytext      | `get_sentiments()`, `inner_join()`                         |
  | Word pairs/correlation | widyr         | `pairwise_count()`, `pairwise_cor()`                       |
  | Plotting               | ggplot2       | `geom_col()`, `geom_point()`                               |

Good luck with the competition.
